# How bacteria are built and get energy

> *A bacterium faces the same problems as one of your cells: it must hold its contents together and
> make ATP. Its solutions explain why a stain turns some bacteria purple and why some bacteria die in
> air.*

## A bacterium and one of your cells {#sec-bact-glance}

Try two questions before you read on. A wrong guess followed by the answer still helps you learn.

<div data-island="quiz" data-src="/quizzes/bacteria-warmup.quiz.yml"></div>

A bacterium is a **prokaryote**: a cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. As the size
ladder in [*The microbial world*](microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-scale) showed, a typical bacterium is
about the size of one of your mitochondria.

The table compares a bacterium with the cells you studied in cell biology. Read the last column with
the sixth question in mind, *what does it have that my cells lack?* Each difference is a possible way
to harm the bacterium without harming you, which is the principle the pharmacology block builds on.

| Feature | Your cells | A bacterium | Why the difference matters later |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | DNA inside a nuclear envelope | No nucleus; one circular chromosome lies free in the cytoplasm | Transcription and translation happen together |
| Mitochondria | Electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane | No mitochondria; electron transport chain in the cell membrane | Bacterial respiration happens at the cell surface |
| Ribosomes | 80S | 70S, smaller and built differently | A target your cytoplasmic ribosomes do not share |
| Cell wall | None | Usually a peptidoglycan wall outside the membrane | A structure with no human equivalent |
| Extra DNA | Mitochondrial DNA only | Often small circles of DNA called plasmids | Plasmids carry genes between bacteria |

[*How bacteria copy themselves and change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd) returns to the differences in
gene expression.

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "bacteria have mitochondria"
Students starting microbiology often credit prokaryotes with mitochondria
[@briggs2017misconceptions]. The slip is understandable, because bacteria do respire, but they
respire on their own cell membrane. The likeness runs the other way: mitochondria descend from
bacteria that came to live inside an ancestral cell, which is why mitochondria have their own
circular DNA and bacterial-type ribosomes.
:::

## The envelope {#sec-bact-envelope}

A bacterium's envelope holds the cell together, controls what enters and leaves, and carries most of
the molecules your immune system recognises.

The cytoplasm of a bacterium is full of dissolved molecules, so water tends to rush in. Without
support, the membrane would swell and burst. The support comes from **peptidoglycan**, a mesh of
sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides that surrounds the whole cell like a string bag
[@silhavy2010envelope]. Human cells make nothing like it.

Most bacteria build their envelope in one of two ways. In **Gram-positive** bacteria, a thick
peptidoglycan wall, many layers deep, lies directly outside the cell membrane, and there is no outer
membrane. In **Gram-negative** bacteria, a thin layer of peptidoglycan lies between the cell membrane
and a second, **outer membrane**, whose outer face is made of **lipopolysaccharide (LPS)**.

The Gram stain, devised by Hans Christian Gram in 1884, reads this difference in a few minutes, and
laboratories still use it to sort most bacteria. Step through it below, and predict the key step
before you see it.

<div data-island="gram-stain" data-src="/diagrams/gram-stain.yml"></div>

### What the envelope means for the host

The difference between the two envelopes matters well beyond the slide.

LPS acts as an alarm signal. Its lipid portion, lipid A, binds immune receptors and drives strong
inflammation: the fever and the dilated, leaky vessels you met in general pathology
[@raetz2002lps]. For this reason LPS is also called **endotoxin**. The immunology block explains the
receptors.

The outer membrane is also a barrier. It keeps out many molecules that reach a Gram-positive cell's
membrane easily, including some drugs.

Peptidoglycan, finally, has no human equivalent, so anything that blocks its construction harms
bacteria and spares your cells.

### Bacteria that fit neither design

*Mycobacterium tuberculosis* has a wall packed with waxy **mycolic acids**. Gram's dyes barely
penetrate it, so mycobacteria are detected with a different method, the **acid-fast stain**. At the
other extreme, *Mycoplasma* has no wall at all. It does not show up on a Gram stain, and anything aimed
at the wall has nothing to act on.

## Shape and arrangement {#sec-bact-shape}

Bacteria come in three basic shapes: **cocci** (spheres), **bacilli** (rods), and curved or spiral
forms. Some stay attached to each other after dividing, in pairs, chains or clusters.

Shape and arrangement are clues to how the cell is built and how it divides, which is the reason to
learn them. The activity below puts two similar organisms side by side. Find what separates them
before the explanation appears.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-staph-strep.yml"></div>

## Capsules, appendages, biofilms and spores {#sec-bact-extras}

Many bacteria carry structures beyond the envelope. Each solves a problem for the bacterium, and each
has a consequence for the host.

| Structure | What it is | What it does for the bacterium | Why it matters to the host |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Capsule** | A slimy outer layer, usually polysaccharide | Hides the cell surface; resists drying | Phagocytes find it hard to engulf ([*Microbes and their hosts*](host-microbe.qmd)) |
| **Pili** (fimbriae) | Short, hair-like protein fibres | Attach the cell to surfaces, including host cells | Attachment is often the first step of colonisation |
| **Flagella** | Long, rotating protein filaments | Swimming towards nutrients | Let bacteria move into new sites |
| **Biofilm** | A community of cells in a shared slime matrix | Shelter from drying, predators and chemicals | Forms on teeth and on medical devices such as catheters |
| **Endospore** | A dormant, dehydrated cell inside protective coats | Survives starvation, heat and chemicals for years | Hard to kill with routine heat or disinfectants |

Spores are made by a few groups of Gram-positive rods, notably *Bacillus* and *Clostridium*. When
nutrients run out, the cell builds a spore inside itself: a copy of its DNA wrapped in a dehydrated
core and several protective coats [@setlow2014spores]. When conditions improve, the spore germinates
back into a growing cell.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Predict: will boiling or an alcohol hand rub kill spores? (Click to check)
Mostly not. Many spores survive boiling at 100 °C, and alcohol hand rubs do not kill them
[@setlow2014spores]. Reliable killing needs pressurised steam at 121 °C, as in an autoclave. This is
why some hospital wards ask staff to wash their hands with soap and water: friction and rinsing
remove spores that alcohol leaves behind. [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](detection-control.qmd#sec-det-control) returns to this.
:::

## Getting energy {#sec-bact-energy}

Bacteria make ATP with the same chemistry as your cells, but with more options. Your cells break down
glucose by glycolysis and pass the electrons down an electron transport chain to oxygen. Many bacteria
use the same two stages, with one difference: oxygen need not be the final electron acceptor.

| Strategy | What happens | Final electron acceptor | ATP per glucose |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Aerobic respiration** | Glycolysis, then an electron transport chain in the cell membrane | Oxygen | High, similar to your cells |
| **Anaerobic respiration** | The same, without oxygen | Another molecule, such as nitrate or sulfate | Lower |
| **Fermentation** | Glycolysis only; pyruvate is converted to products such as lactate or ethanol | None; no electron transport chain | Low, about 2 |

Your own skeletal muscle ferments glucose to lactate during a sprint, when oxygen supply cannot keep
up. Some bacteria live this way all the time.

## The oxygen spectrum {#sec-bact-oxygen}

Oxygen is the most effective electron acceptor available, but it is also chemically dangerous.
Partly reduced oxygen forms **reactive oxygen species**, such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide,
which damage proteins and DNA. You met these as by-products of your own mitochondria.

Every bacterium therefore has two answers to give: *can it use oxygen to make ATP*, and *does oxygen
harm it?* Together the answers place it in one of five groups.

| Group | Uses oxygen to make ATP? | Harmed by normal air? | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Obligate aerobe** | Yes, and has no alternative | No | *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* |
| **Facultative anaerobe** | Yes, when oxygen is present; ferments otherwise | No | *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus* |
| **Microaerophile** | Yes, but only at low oxygen levels | Yes, at atmospheric levels | *Campylobacter jejuni* |
| **Aerotolerant anaerobe** | No; ferments only | No; it has protective enzymes | Streptococci, *Lactobacillus* |
| **Obligate anaerobe** | No | Yes | *Bacteroides fragilis*, *Clostridium* species |

There is no need to memorise the table. If you know how an organism handles energy and oxygen, you can
work out where it will grow. In the activity below, each organism is described only by its metabolism,
and its name appears after you choose.

<div data-island="oxygen-tube" data-src="/diagrams/oxygen-tube.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "anaerobes die because they lack catalase and superoxide dismutase"
Older textbooks explain oxygen toxicity this way, extrapolating from an observation made in the
1970s. Many anaerobes do carry these protective enzymes; *Bacteroides fragilis*, for example, makes
both. Oxygen kills anaerobes by damaging the machinery they depend on: central enzymes built around
exposed iron–sulfur clusters or radical chemistry, which oxygen and reactive oxygen species
inactivate directly [@lu2021anaerobes].
:::

### Oxygen in the body

Your body has oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor sites. Skin and airways are exposed to air. The colon
contains almost no oxygen, and anaerobes there outnumber facultative bacteria many times over.
Oxygen-poor sites also appear when tissue loses its blood supply: **ischaemic** (poorly perfused) and
necrotic tissue, and the centre of an abscess, contain little oxygen and suit anaerobes.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-ecoli-bacteroides.yml"></div>

## Growth {#sec-bact-growth}

Bacteria reproduce by **binary fission**: the cell copies its chromosome, grows, and splits in two.
The time this takes is the **doubling time**. In ideal laboratory conditions *E. coli* doubles about
every 20 minutes, while *M. tuberculosis* takes most of a day.

Starting from $N_0$ cells, after time $t$ with doubling time $g$:

$$ N = N_0 \times 2^{t/g} $$

One *E. coli* cell doubling every 20 minutes becomes about 17 million cells in 8 hours, which is 24
doublings. *M. tuberculosis* takes weeks to form a visible colony, so its culture also takes weeks.

In a closed container, a population passes through four phases:

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| Lag | Cells adjust to new conditions; little division |
| Exponential (log) | Steady doubling, as in the equation above |
| Stationary | Nutrients run low and waste accumulates; division and death balance |
| Death | More cells die than divide |

Rapidly dividing cells are the most vulnerable to many antimicrobial drugs, a point the pharmacology
block returns to.

## Two microbe profiles {#sec-bact-profiles}

Every organism in this book gets the same five-slot card: *identity and structure*, *lifestyle and
niche*, *mechanism of harm*, *general consequence*, and a *contrast partner* it is easily confused
with. The organ-system blocks will later add where it infects, how it is diagnosed and how it is
treated; the card gives those facts somewhere to go.

The first card below has three slots filled in, and you predict the other two. The second has one.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-s-aureus.yml"></div>

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-b-fragilis.yml"></div>

The two cards have a lot in common. Both organisms live harmlessly on or in many healthy people
[@kluytmans1997carriage], and both cause harm mainly when they reach a site where they do not
belong. Both tend to cause **pyogenic** (pus-forming) infection and abscesses, and the capsule of
*B. fragilis* actively promotes abscess formation [@tzianabos1993abscess]. Their differences come
from this chapter's two questions: one envelope design or the other, and tolerance of oxygen or not.

## The trait toolkit {#sec-bact-toolkit}

The traits in this chapter are the toolkit that every later chapter uses to describe a bacterium.

| Trait | The options | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Envelope | Gram-positive, Gram-negative, acid-fast (waxy), no wall | Whether the immune system meets LPS; what can enter the cell; whether drugs aimed at the wall can act |
| Shape and arrangement | Cocci, rods, curved or spiral; clusters, chains, pairs | Clues to identity and to how the cell divides |
| Additional structures | Capsule, pili, flagella, biofilm, spores | How it attaches, moves, hides and survives outside a host |
| Energy and oxygen | Aerobe, facultative, microaerophile, aerotolerant, anaerobe | Where in the body it can live; how a sample must be handled |
| Growth rate | Doubling in minutes, or in about a day | How fast an infection develops; how long culture takes |

[*How bacteria copy themselves and change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd) takes up the third question, and
[*Microbes and their hosts*](host-microbe.qmd) the fifth.
